blocks.text: 1. Underfitting

blocks.alt: Low training accuracy with also low validation accuracy signals underfitting

blocks.text: Overfitting, the previous topic, described a model that learns too much from training data, effectively memorizing it rather than genuinely learning from it. Underfitting is the genuinely opposite problem: a model that fails to learn the actual pattern at all.

Both are genuine failures of generalization, just in opposite directions, and understanding both clearly, side by side, gives a genuinely complete picture of what actually goes wrong when a network fails to train well.
2. What Underfitting Actually Is
Underfitting means a network fails to capture even the genuine, underlying pattern present in the training data itself, a genuinely more fundamental failure than overfitting.

This produces poor performance on the training data itself, not just on new, unseen data, directly connecting back to Network Architecture's own capacity concept, already covered in the Neural Network Fundamentals module, since insufficient capacity is often the genuine, structural root cause.
3. The Train-Validation Signal for Underfitting

blocks.alt: Both curves staying flat and high is the underfitting signal

blocks.text: This connects back to the train-validation gap already covered in the Overfitting topic. Overfitting produces a genuine, widening gap between training and validation performance, with training performance genuinely good and validation genuinely not.

Underfitting instead produces both training and validation performance being genuinely, similarly poor, with no meaningful gap at all between the two, since neither has actually learned much of anything genuinely useful.

blocks.text: 4. Genuinely Common Causes

blocks.alt: A too simple model and not enough training both cause underfitting

blocks.text: A network with genuinely too little capacity for the problem's real, actual complexity is a common cause, directly connecting back to Network Architecture's own capacity concept, already covered in its own dedicated topic.

Training stopped genuinely too early, before the network has actually learned enough, connects forward to Early Stopping, covered later in this module, and a learning rate that is genuinely too small, or too much regularization already being applied, both covered further later in this module, are two additional, common causes worth knowing.
5. The Capacity Connection

blocks.alt: A low capacity model cannot learn the real pattern

blocks.text: This connects back to a network's total parameter count, already covered in the Weights and Biases topic. A genuinely too-small network simply cannot represent the actual, real complexity a given problem genuinely requires, regardless of how well that small network actually gets trained.

No amount of additional training time can fix this specific, structural limitation, a genuinely important distinction from other, more fixable causes of underfitting already covered in the previous section.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Training a genuinely undersized network for considerably longer is a common, well-intentioned but ultimately ineffective response to underfitting. If the root cause is genuinely insufficient capacity, only increasing that capacity actually helps.

blocks.text: 6. A Genuinely Useful Visual Intuition

This connects back to the visual intuition already covered in the Overfitting topic. An underfit model produces a genuinely oversimplified boundary, missing real, actual structure that genuinely exists within the data.

A straight line drawn through data that genuinely, visibly curves is a classic, clear illustration of exactly this problem, the model's own representational capacity simply too limited to capture the curve that is genuinely, actually there.
7. Fixing Underfitting

blocks.alt: Underfitting gets fixed by adding capacity or training longer

blocks.text: The genuinely direct fixes include increasing the network's own capacity, more layers or more neurons, directly connecting back to Network Architecture, already covered in its own dedicated topic.

Training for genuinely more epochs, already covered in The Deep Learning Workflow topic, and reducing regularization strength if any is genuinely already being applied, covered further later in this module, are two additional, genuinely direct fixes worth trying depending on the specific, actual root cause already identified.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Root cause","Direct fix"],"rows":[["Insufficient network capacity","Add more layers or neurons"],["Training stopped too early","Train for more epochs"],["Too much regularization already applied","Reduce its strength"]]}

blocks.text: 8. The Real, Shared Tradeoff

blocks.alt: Underfitting from being too simple trades off against overfitting from being too complex

blocks.text: This connects forward to the Bias-Variance Tradeoff, the very next topic in this module. Overfitting and Underfitting sit at genuinely opposite ends of one single, shared spectrum, not two entirely separate, unrelated problems.

Fixing one, taken too far, can genuinely push a model directly toward the other, exactly why the next topic in this module frames both of these problems together, as two sides of one single, genuinely unified tradeoff.
9. Recognizing Underfitting in a Real Training Run

blocks.alt: Both losses staying high and flat confirms underfitting

blocks.text: Both training and validation accuracy being genuinely, similarly low, already covered throughout this topic, is a direct, clear signal to increase capacity or training time, rather than to add more regularization, which would only make underfitting genuinely worse.

This is precisely why correctly distinguishing overfitting from underfitting, covered throughout this topic and the previous one, genuinely matters before actually reaching for any specific fix, since the two problems call for genuinely, directly opposite kinds of responses.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates underfitting, training a genuinely oversimplified model on a curved dataset and observing both training and validation performance staying poor.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = np.linspace(-3, 3, 200).reshape(-1, 1)
y = np.sin(X.ravel()) + rng.normal(scale=0.1, size=200)

X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

# A deliberately, genuinely oversimplified model for this genuinely curved pattern
underfitting_model = MLPRegressor(hidden_layer_sizes=(1,), max_iter=200, random_state=42)
underfitting_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

train_score = underfitting_model.score(X_train, y_train)
val_score = underfitting_model.score(X_val, y_val)

print(f"Training R-squared score: {train_score:.4f}")
print(f"Validation R-squared score: {val_score:.4f}")
print(f"\nGap between training and validation: {train_score - val_score:.4f}")
print("Notice BOTH scores are genuinely low, with no meaningful gap, exactly the underfitting pattern covered in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This example deliberately uses a genuinely tiny single-neuron hidden layer for a curved, sine-wave pattern, exactly the insufficient-capacity cause already covered in this topic, producing poor performance on both training and validation data alike.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Underfitting is the genuinely opposite problem from overfitting, a model that fails to learn the pattern at all.
It produces poor performance on the training data itself, not just on new, unseen data.
Both training and validation performance are genuinely, similarly poor, with no meaningful gap between the two.
Common causes include insufficient network capacity, premature stopping, or an overly cautious setup.
A genuinely too-small network cannot represent a problem's real complexity, and more training time alone cannot fix this.
An underfit model produces a genuinely oversimplified boundary, missing real structure that exists in the data.
Direct fixes include increasing capacity, training for more epochs, or reducing regularization strength.
Overfitting and Underfitting sit at opposite ends of one shared spectrum, not two entirely separate problems.
Next up: Bias-Variance Tradeoff, framing both of these problems together as one single, unified concept.
